cards.text: Friend, meet Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles by the Kebar River in the land of the Chaldeans (Ezekiel 1:1-3). He tells this one himself, so every "me" is Ezekiel. In the ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD comes to him.

cards.question: God starts Ezekiel off with a writing job. What does He tell Ezekiel to write down?
God tells Ezekiel why the date matters. On this very day, the king of Babylon has laid siege to ___.

cards.text: Now God tells Ezekiel to speak a parable to this rebellious house, and to tell them what the Lord GOD says.

cards.question: The first thing God says in the parable is to put a pot on the fire and pour in water.
With the water in, God names the meat that goes into the pot. Which pieces?

cards.text: Take the choicest of the flock, pile the fuel beneath the pot, bring it to a boil and cook the bones. Friend, that's the cooking version of me breaking out the GOOD chocolate chips, the ones I hide behind the flour so I can't find them at midnight.
Then the Lord GOD speaks again, and it starts with a woe to the city of bloodshed. Friend, that city is the pot.

cards.question: God says something is wrong with this pot. What is it?

answers.text: It's rusted and the rust won't come off
It's cracked straight down the side
It's far too small to hold the meat

cards.question: When the pot is emptied piece by piece, God says to cast lots for what comes out.

cards.text: This part's heavy, friend. God says the blood the city shed is still within her.

cards.question: Where does God say the city poured out the blood she shed?
The city poured that blood on the ground and covered it with dust.
God says He placed her blood on the bare rock so it would not be covered. Why does He say He did it?

answers.text: To stir up wrath and take vengeance
To warn the nations all around
To call the priests to pray

cards.text: Back to the pot, friend, and that line again: "Woe to the city of bloodshed!" Then the Lord GOD says, "I, too, will pile the kindling high."
Logs piled on, fire kindled, meat cooked well, spices mixed in. I cranked an oven that high ONE time, friend, and the smoke alarm didn't even beep. It just quietly packed a bag and LEFT.

cards.question: With the fire roaring like that, what does God say about the bones in the pot?

cards.text: Then the empty pot goes onto the coals until it gets hot and its copper glows.

cards.question: What does God say all that heat will do to the empty pot?

answers.text: Melt its impurity and burn off its rust
Make it shine bright for a feast
Harden it so it never cracks

cards.question: God says the pot has frustrated every effort so far. Even the fire has removed its thick rust.

cards.text: Friend, I KNOW that kind of pan: midnight, sticky cookie sheet, I soak it, I scrub it, I give it a whole PEP TALK, and NOTHING. Then God stops describing the pot and starts saying "you."

cards.question: In the parable, God stops describing the rusted pot and speaks to "you." He says: Because of the indecency of your uncleanness I tried to ___ you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness.
God keeps speaking to the one He tried to cleanse. He says: You will not be pure again until when?

answers.text: Until the king of Babylon leaves
Until you bring a new offering

cards.text: Then God closes it out: "I, the LORD, have spoken; the time is coming, and I will act."

cards.question: God says He may still relent and hold back.
Closing out the parable, God says to the one He tried to cleanse: I will judge you according to what?

findings.problem: The stop goes beyond a few discovery questions. After the opening discoveries about the date and Jerusalem, cards 5, 6, 9 and 10 still require guesses about the parable's first action, the meat, the pot's defect and casting lots. The earlier cards do not provide enough context to reason out those answers, so most of this stop's choices rely on luck rather than informed reasoning.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: This non-opening story card has three sentences: the passage summary followed by two sentences for the smoke-alarm joke.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.
